title: Parametric DRAG for leakage-suppressed exchange gates in superconducting qubits
authors: Yiwen Li, Xinsheng Tan, Yang Yu
abstract: Programmable exchange interactions support quantum gates and many-body simulation in superconducting circuits. Fast excitation transfer, however, opens two leakage pathways in weakly anharmonic transmons, degrading gates and driving simulated dynamics outside the encoded state space. We introduce parametric derivative removal by adiabatic gate (PDRAG) to suppress both pathways while preserving the target exchange. Their conjugate structure determines first- and second-derivative corrections implemented through one real frequency command. At $g/2π=100$ MHz, calibrated PDRAG achieves a geometric-mean leakage reduction of $5.27\times10^5$ relative to the base pulse across 12.5--35 ns in Duffing simulations. At 13 ns, endpoint leakage reaches $1.98\times10^{-7}$ for the calibrated full-exchange pulse. Transferring the derivative coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian gives a mean 893-fold reduction over 12.5--22 ns after amplitude and carrier recalibration. Floquet return interference and charge-induced gap shifts explain the calibration and transfer gains, connecting compact pulse design to leakage-suppressed programmable interactions.
summary: This paper introduces Parametric DRAG (PDRAG) to suppress leakage in superconducting qubit exchange gates. By controlling both the first and second derivatives of the pulse envelope, the technique significantly reduces unwanted leakage channels. This advancement is crucial for building reliable quantum processors by enabling high-fidelity gate operations.
main_problem: The primary challenge is suppressing leakage pathways in superconducting qubits while maintaining the fidelity of fast quantum exchange gates.
main_result: The proposed Parametric DRAG (PDRAG) technique achieves significant leakage suppression, demonstrating geometric-mean reductions up to $5.27 	imes 10^5$ compared to base pulses.
method: The method involves designing the pulse using derivative control (first and second derivatives) applied to the exchange interaction envelope, which is then calibrated to minimize leakage.
model_or_system: The system is based on superconducting qubits modeled by weakly anharmonic transmons, described by a Duffing oscillator Hamiltonian. The control is implemented via frequency excursions.
key_observables: Leakage coefficients ($L_{11}$), gate fidelity ($L$, $1-F_{fSim}$), and the achieved suppression gain ($S$).
important_parameters: Gate duration (12.5–35 ns), coupling strength ($g/2\pi=100$ MHz), and the derivative coefficients ($ eta, \gamma$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of the rotating-wave approximation and relies on complex calibration procedures to tune derivative coefficients.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction of PDRAG, comparing leakage dynamics across different pulse protocols (Base vs. Calibrated PDRAG) and showing the spectral content of the control fields.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of leakage in fast gates, details the PDRAG method using derivative control, presents quantitative results showing massive leakage suppression across various gate times, and finally discusses transferring the optimized coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian model.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly practical and numerically rigorous method for designing control pulses for superconducting qubits, directly addressing a major bottleneck (leakage) in realizing high-fidelity quantum gates.
